Neonatal individuals of the South American sea lion emerge at a modest size, with female pups measuring approximately 79 centimeters [Lb = approximately 79 centimeters] in length at birth and male pups averaging about 82 centimeters [Lb = about 82 centimeters]. This subtle sexual dimorphism in neonatal length is consistent with patterns observed across otariid lineages, where males are typically slightly larger even at the moment of parturition. The corresponding body masses at birth also reflect this early divergence: female neonates weigh roughly 12.3 kilograms [Wwb = roughly 12.3 kilograms], while their male counterparts tip the scales at around 13.5 kilograms [Wwb = around 13.5 kilograms]. These values, derived from field measurements taken on rookeries along the Patagonian coast, provide a baseline for assessing neonatal condition and early growth trajectories. The modest birth mass belies the rapid somatic development that ensues during the nursing period, a phase characterized by intense maternal investment through prolonged lactation. Environmental conditions during this vulnerable neonatal stage can substantially influence survival probabilities, particularly in years of reduced prey availability that constrain maternal foraging efficiency and, consequently, milk production.

The gestation period in Otaria flavescens, measured under the standard core body temperature typical of eutherian mammals at rest, 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], extends for approximately 357 days [tg = approximately 357 days]. This duration includes a period of embryonic diapause, a common reproductive strategy among otariids that allows for the synchronization of parturition with favorable environmental conditions on land. Following birth, the offspring remain entirely dependent on maternal milk for a substantial interval, and the time since birth at weaning is observed to be roughly 365 days since birth [tx = roughly 365 days since birth] under the same reference body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended nursing period, lasting a full year in many cases, is among the longest recorded for any pinniped species and reflects the challenging marine foraging environment faced by lactating females. Pups gradually begin to consume solid prey alongside milk during their second year, but nutritional independence is a protracted process. The interplay between gestation length and weaning timing is critical for understanding the overall pace of life history in this species, placing it at the slow end of the otariid reproductive continuum.

Sexual maturation in this species is markedly delayed compared to many other marine mammals, a trait that underscores its relatively slow life-history strategy. Under the species' normal core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], females typically reach puberty at approximately 1,461 days since birth [tp = approximately 1,461 days since birth], which equates to roughly four years of age. Males, in contrast, attain sexual maturity significantly later, with puberty recorded at around 2,191 days since birth [tp = around 2,191 days since birth], or about six years of age, under the same thermal conditions. This pronounced sex-based divergence in maturation timing is a common feature of polygynous pinniped societies, where males must delay reproduction to acquire the size and social capital necessary to defend a territory and secure access to estrous females. The onset of gonadal activity in young males is therefore not merely a physiological milestone but also a social one, contingent upon successful competition with older, larger conspecifics. These developmental timelines have been corroborated by longitudinal studies of known-age individuals in colonies across Uruguay and Argentina.

Adult body size in the South American sea lion exhibits one of the most extreme cases of sexual dimorphism among the otariids. Females reach an ultimate total length of around 200 centimeters [Li = around 200 centimeters] and attain a maximum wet weight of approximately 150 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 150 kilograms], a formidable size for a female pinniped. Males, however, grow to be substantially larger, with an ultimate total length of about 250 centimeters [Li = about 250 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight reaching up to 350 kilograms [Wwi = up to 350 kilograms]. This dramatic size disparity is intimately linked to the species' polygynous mating system, where large body size confers a decisive advantage in male-male combat over breeding territories on crowded rookeries. The allometric scaling of skeletal and muscular mass in males requires an extended period of somatic growth well beyond the onset of sexual maturity, meaning that many young males are physiologically capable of reproduction long before they are socially competitive. The energetic demands of achieving and maintaining such massive body size also shape foraging ecology, with adult males often diving deeper and traveling farther than females.

The maximum lifespan of Otaria flavescens under natural conditions, recorded at a reference core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], has been estimated at approximately 29 years [am = approximately 29 years], based on long-term mark-recapture studies and tooth annuli analysis of senescent individuals. This longevity, while modest compared to some phocid seals, is considerable for an otariid and permits multiple reproductive episodes over a lifetime. The theoretical maximum reproductive rate for the species, calculated at the same standard metabolic temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], corresponds to one pup per year [Ri = one pup per year]. Interbirth intervals are occasionally extended to two years following years of poor foraging conditions, illustrating the flexibility inherent in this life-history system. The combination of extended lifespan, delayed maturation, and low annual reproductive output conforms to a typical K-selected strategy, optimizing survival and offspring quality in a variable marine environment where adult mortality is relatively low.
